title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations

paper.title: Sparse-TD-JEPA: Improving Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning With Sparse Latent Task Representations
paper.abstract:
Abstract Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset.
We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow.
We address this limitation by introducing an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder’s latent space.
The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure.
We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA , a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning.
We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation.
Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons.
On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 ± 6 661\pm 6 to 714 ± 3 714\pm 3 .
On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 ± 0.8 38.0\pm 0.8 to 48.4 ± 2.3 48.4\pm 2.3 , with improvements of 13.4–18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains.
Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains.
Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape, offering a mechanistic explanation for the observed performance gains.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Zero-shot reinforcement learning studies the problem of pre-training a single policy on offline, reward-free data such that it can solve any downstream task without further interaction with the environment. It is important because it scales the achievable tasks of a single model without requiring an equal amount of scaling to the training data or online experience, making RL more practical across the diverse and open-ended settings encountered in the real world. A prominent line of work addresses this problem through successor features and task encoders, where a latent representation of states is learned such that any reward function can be expressed as a linear function of that representation Barreto et al. (2017) ; Touati and Ollivier (2021) . At test time, a small set of labeled transitions suffices to recover a task vector via linear regression, which is then used to retrieve the corresponding pre-trained policy. Recent zero-shot RL methods have explored a diverse range of objectives for constructing task representations. Laplacian representations capture the geometry of the environment through eigenfunctions of its transition graph Wu et al. (2018) , while ICVF learns representations through intention-conditioned value prediction Ghosh et al. (2023) . HILP instead organizes the latent space around temporal distances for goal reaching Park et al. (2024) . Self-predictive approaches such as BYOL and BYOL- γ \gamma have also been adapted to the successor-feature setting by predicting future latent representations over one or multiple time scales Grill et al. (2020) ; Lawson et al. (2025) . More recent methods, including RLDP and TD-JEPA, improve multi-step latent-dynamics prediction through chained or temporal-difference objectives Jajoo et al. (2026) ; Bagatella et al. (2025) . Although these approaches differ in how they learn task-relevant structure, they all ultimately rely on the learned task representation to support accurate linear reward inference at test time. Despite this progress, a critical bottleneck has received comparatively little attention. When the task encoder spreads reward-predictive information diffusely across all latent dimensions, the predicted reward landscape is less concentrated near the goal. The resulting reward signal has a weaker gradient to follow, leading to degraded downstream performance. We find that this difference in landscape sharpness persists across a wide range of labeled-set sizes, suggesting it reflects a structural property of the encoder geometry. We address these challenges through a sparsity penalty for the task encoding representation to concentrate its reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of its latent space. We instantiate this idea as Sparse-TD-JEPA , a single-line code addition based on TD-JEPA framework that significantly improves performance on various navigation, locomotion, and puzzle tasks. Empirically, this simple modification produces consistent gains across all 13 evaluated domain-level comparisons. On DeepMind-Control (DMC) , Sparse TD-JEPA improves the average return from 661 ± 6 661\pm 6 to 714 ± 3 714\pm 3 , a gain of 53 points. On OGBench , it raises the average success rate from 38.0 ± 0.8 38.0\pm 0.8 to 48.4 ± 2.3 48.4\pm 2.3 , an absolute improvement of 10.4 percentage points. Moreover, analysis experiment shows that the resulting encoder produces a sharper, more peaked predicted reward landscape, giving the downstream policy a clearer signal to follow. Our contributions are as follows: • We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that ℓ 1 \ell_{1} sparsity on the task encoder improves zero-shot reinforcement learning performance. • Through controlled analysis experiments, we show that the sparsity-penalized task encoder produces a smoother and more informative reward landscape. • We evaluate our method across standard zero-shot reinforcement learning benchmarks covering robotic locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks. We demonstrate consistent gains over the base method and other established zero-shot baselines.

sections.heading: Latent-predictive representation learning.
sections.text: The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) LeCun and others (2022) is a representations learning architecture that splits an input into a context view and a target view, then trains a predictor to map the context encoding to the target encoding in a shared latent space. This principle has been instantiated across modalities. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) Assran et al. (2023) applies it to static images. It uses an asymmetric context/target-encoder design to predict the representations of masked image regions from visible patches. Video-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) Bardes et al. (2024) ; Assran et al. (2025) extends this to video. It predicts masked spatio-temporal tokens from unmasked ones and supports downstream robotic planning without task-specific reward. Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) Bagatella et al. (2025) instantiates the same context-target prediction problem in reinforcement learning. A state encoder and a task encoder are trained via a temporal-difference latent-predictive loss over offline, off-policy transitions. The predictor is conditioned on the action and a policy latent.

sections.heading: Zero-shot reinforcement learning.
sections.text: Zero-shot Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods are methods that pre-train an agent once on offline, reward-free data, then at test time solve arbitrary downstream tasks without further interaction. Most zero-shot RL methods learn a task encoder alongside successor features . The task encoder maps states to a space in which any reward is linear. The successor features predict how much of each task-encoder dimension a policy accumulates over time. Forward-Backward (FB) representations Touati and Ollivier (2021) , a zero-shot RL method, learns both jointly via a bilinear decomposition of successor measures. Other zero-shot reinforcement learning methods construct the task encoder through different objectives. Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) Grill et al. (2020) predicts an encoder’s own future latents. The Laplacian representation Wu et al. (2018) uses eigenfunctions of the environment’s transition graph. The Intention-Conditioned Value Function (ICVF) Ghosh et al. (2023) method uses an implicit value-based objective. HILbert foundation Policy (HILP) Park et al. (2024) enforces distance-preservation for goal-reaching. Regularized Latent Dynamics Prediction (RLDP) Jajoo et al. (2026) uses chained multi-step latent prediction. BYOL- γ \gamma Lawson et al. (2025) extends BYOL to multi-step targets. TD-JEPA Bagatella et al. (2025) uses a temporal-difference latent-predictive objective as the core training signal for both encoders. It distills zero-shot policies end to end.

sections.heading: Sparse and structured representation learning.
sections.text: Sparsity-inducing penalties encourage weights or activations toward zero. We refer to Hoefler et al. (2021) for a survey. A useful distinction is between model sparsity , which permanently removes structural elements, and ephemeral sparsity , which sparsifies activations per-example without altering the architecture. Dropout Srivastava et al. (2014) applies ephemeral sparsity to hidden units for regularization. k k -sparse autoencoders Makhzani and Frey (2013) retain only the top- k k activations per example for unsupervised feature learning. Closer to our motivation, Liu et al. (2019) show that ephemeral sparsity in the last hidden layer of a control network improves value-function learning on classic control tasks. It reduces activation overlap between unrelated states. This mitigates interference during bootstrapping. It is evidence that sparsity can directly aid the kind of TD-based learning our method builds on.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Setup
sections.text: We consider a Markov Decision Process (MDP) ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , R , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R,\gamma) , where 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is the action space, P ⁡ ( s ′ ∣ s , a ) P(s^{\prime}\mid s,a) is the transition kernel, giving the probability measure over the next state s ′ s^{\prime} when action a a is taken in state s s , R ⁡ ( s , a ) R(s,a) is the reward function, and γ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \gamma\in[0,1] is the discount factor, giving down-weights rewards received further in the future ( Sutton et al., 1998 ; Touati and Ollivier, 2021 ) . sections.heading: 4 Method: Sparse TD-JEPA
sections.text: We propose to induce per-example sparsity in the projected task embeddings project ​ _ ​ z ​ ( ψ ⁡ ( s ) ) \mathrm{project\_z}(\psi(s)) during training, encouraging each embedding to concentrate its mass on fewer strongly active dimensions. The intended effect is that reward-predictive information occupies a smaller effective subspace of ψ \psi ’s output, so that least-squares inference recovers z r z_{r} as a direction aligned with that subspace, producing a sharper, more concentrated inferred reward landscape with a stronger signal for the downstream policy to follow. We note that Eq. equation 5 constrains each embedding individually and does not by itself force different states to share a support; whether a shared low-dimensional structure emerges is an empirical question, which we probe directly in the experiments (via the inferred reward landscape and its correlation with task progress) rather than assume. Because the encoder output is constrained to the sphere of radius d ψ \sqrt{d_{\psi}} , the ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty cannot shrink the magnitude of the representation; on the sphere, ‖ x ‖ 1 \|x\|_{1} is minimized exactly by coordinate-sparse directions, so the penalty purely reorients embeddings toward sparser directions rather than acting as a generic shrinkage regularizer.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We design our experiments to answer the following research questions: • RQ1: Does inducing sparsity in the task encoder improve zero-shot performance over the dense TD-JEPA baseline and established zero-shot RL methods, across locomotion, navigation, object manipulation, and puzzle-solving benchmarks? • RQ2: Does sparsity produce a sharper, more spatially concentrated predicted reward signal near the goal, and does this explain the stuck-policy failure mode observed with the dense encoder? • RQ3: How does the sharpness of the inferred reward signal depend on the size of the labeled-set N N used for zero-shot inference, and does our method retain its advantage across different inference budgets? sections.heading: 5.1 Environments and Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate our method on two comprehensive offline reinforcement learning benchmark suites: DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) Tassa et al. (2018) ; Tunyasuvunakool et al. (2020) and Offline Goal-Conditioned RL Benchmark (OGBench) Park et al. (2025) , both are popular in recent zero-shot RL literature Lawson et al. (2025) ; Park et al. (2024) ; Jajoo et al. (2026) . All datasets are publicly available and are used as-is in our experiments. DMC is a MuJoCo environment with locomotion tasks spanning walker , cheetah , quadruped , and pointmass domains. We evaluate our method on all four domains across 20 tasks, each trained on 3 million environment steps of interaction. For training, we use the offline data set constructed with the EXploratory data for Offline Reinforcement Learning (ExoRL) protocol Yarats et al. (2022) . For zero-shot evaluation, we execute 10 independent rollouts per task and report the average return. OGBench is a MuJoCo RL benchmark with various locomotion, navigation, object manipulation, robotic arm manipulation, and puzzle-solving tasks. We evaluate our method on nine OGBench domains, each with 5 tasks, for a total of 45 different tasks. We use the Antmaze domain for navigation, goal-stitching, and exploration Park et al. (2025) , the Scene and Puzzle domains for puzzle-solving locomotion, and the Cube Single and Cube Double domains for object manipulation tasks using robotic arm. For each domain, our model is trained on 1 million environment steps of offline interaction. For zero-shot evaluation, we execute 10 independent rollouts per task and report the average return. Performance is measured as the success rate of the binary outcome in each rollout Park et al. (2025) .

sections.heading: 5.2 Baselines
sections.text: We compare our method against eight zero-shot RL baselines: Laplacian Wu et al. (2018) , ICVF Ghosh et al. (2023) , HILP Park et al. (2024) , FB Touati and Ollivier (2021) , RLDP Jajoo et al. (2026) , BYOL Grill et al. (2020) , BYOL- γ \gamma Lawson et al. (2025) , and TD-JEPA Bagatella et al. (2025) . Each baseline is tuned over its own per-domain grid of learning rates and orthonormality (or goal-sampling) coefficients to ensure a fair comparison. ICVF, BYOL, BYOL- γ \gamma are representation-learning objectives not originally proposed for zero-shot RL. We use the public codebase of Bagatella et al. (2025) , which contains the adaptation of these methods for the tasks in our experiments.

sections.heading: 5.3 Computing And Environment Infrastructure
sections.text: OGBench experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H200 NVL GPU (141GB HBM3e), with an Intel Xeon 6960P (Granite Rapids) CPU, 754GB system RAM, and Linux (kernel 5.14, RHEL 9-family). DMC experiments were run on a single NVIDIA H100 NVL GPU (94GB HBM3), with an AMD EPYC 9454 (48-Core) CPU, 594GB system RAM, and Linux (kernel 5.15, Ubuntu 22.04-family). All experiments used Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.9 (CUDA 12.8), with gymnasium 1.2, ogbench 1.2, MuJoCo 3.3, NumPy 2.3, pandas 2.3, and scikit-learn 1.9.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We identified an underexplored failure mode of successor-feature-based zero-shot RL, dense task encoders yield a diffuse inferred reward signal with little contrast between goal-relevant states and the background, and addressed it with a simple one-line ℓ 1 \ell_{1} penalty on TD-JEPA’s projected task embeddings, which provably controls only the effective dimensionality of the representation and leaves the closed-form inference procedure untouched. Sparse TD-JEPA improves over the dense baseline in almost every evaluated domain, and our analyses tie these gains to a sharper, more goal-concentrated inferred reward that persists across labeled-set sizes. Future work includes applying the sparsity penalty to other successor-feature-based zero-shot RL methods beyond TD-JEPA, and leveraging the resulting sparse, low-effective-dimension task embeddings for mechanistic interpretability of what individual latent dimensions encode.

sections.heading: Appendix B Qualitative Rollout Analysis of the Stuck-Policy Failure Mode
sections.text: RQ2 in the main paper’s Experiments section asks whether the sharper, sparsity-induced reward landscape explains the stuck-policy failure mode we observe with the dense TD-JEPA baseline. Figures 6 – 8 give concrete, single-episode illustrations of what this failure mode looks like in practice. The systematic evidence for the hypothesis itself remains the aggregate correlation results reported in the main experiment, across all seeds and domains. Each figure shows one evaluation episode for a fully trained model, comparing Sparse TD-JEPA ( Ours , top row) against the dense TD-JEPA baseline ( bottom row ) on the same task, seeded with the same evaluation seed. Reward Landscape shows the spatial reward-landscape: colour encodes z r ⊤ ​ ψ ​ ( s ) z_{r}^{\top}\psi(s) normalized by each model’s own mean predicted reward for far-field states ( > 10 >10 m from goal), with the goal marked by a star and dotted rings at 1 m, 3 m, and 5 m. Rollout overlays the agent’s actual trajectory on the maze, coloured by its own learned value estimate V ⁡ ( s ) = ψ ​ ( s ) ⊤ ​ z r V(s)=\psi(s)^{\top}z_{r} along the path (red = low, green = high). Value Convergence vs. Distance to Goal plots V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) and the Euclidean distance-to-goal against timestep, together with their ordinary-least-squares trend lines; Task Success marks with a check or cross whether the episode reached the goal. We highlight two recurring, related instances of this failure mode below.

sections.heading: B.1 Failure Mode 1: Flat Value Signal
sections.text: One failure mode we observed empirically is that the dense baseline often never acquires enough signal to leave the vicinity of its start state at all. As an example, Figures 6 and 7 show one full episode each on antmaze-large-stitch and antmaze-medium-navigate. In both cases the sparse agent’s distance-to-goal decreases steadily over the episode while V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) rises correspondingly, reaching the goal well before the episode times out. The dense baseline, by contrast, remains confined to a small region near its starting position for the entire episode: its distance-to-goal trend is essentially flat, and its V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) trace is noisy with no discernible trend. Figure 6: Full antmaze-large-stitch episode (task 4). Sparse TD-JEPA navigates from its start position to the goal, with V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) rising and distance-to-goal falling together over the episode. The dense TD-JEPA baseline instead loops within a small region far from the goal for the entire episode, never making net progress, and fails. Figure 7: Full antmaze-medium-navigate episode (task 4). Sparse TD-JEPA reaches the goal directly from its start position. The dense TD-JEPA baseline remains tangled in a small loop immediately around its start position for the full episode and fails to make progress toward the goal.

sections.heading: B.2 Failure Mode 2: Diffuse Reward Signal Near the Goal
sections.text: A related instance of the same underlying issue occurs even when the dense baseline does make it near the goal. The predicted reward stays elevated across most of the goal room rather than peaking sharply at the goal itself, giving the policy little local gradient to follow. As an example, Figure 8 shows the last five metres of one such episode on the antmaze-large-stitch task. The sparse agent’s V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) rises steadily as distance-to-goal falls, and it reaches the goal. The dense baseline’s V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) instead fluctuates without a clear upward trend even as it moves in and out of the goal room, and it visibly doubles back on its own path near the goal rather than committing to it; the episode times out without success. This is consistent with the diffuse reward landscape reported in the main paper’s Experiments section: near the goal, small differences in position are not reflected in V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) for the dense encoder, so the policy has no local signal telling it exactly where to stop. Figure 8: Last five metres of an antmaze-large-stitch episode (task 4). Rollout zoomed to the 10 m × \times 10 m region centred on the goal. Sparse TD-JEPA’s value estimate V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) rises monotonically as it closes the remaining distance and succeeds; the dense TD-JEPA baseline’s V ⁡ ( s ) V(s) is noisy and directionless over the same last-mile window, even dropping sharply to near zero at one point, and the agent wanders near the goal room without ever committing to the goal, ultimately failing the episode.

We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder’s latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA , a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 ± 6 661\pm 6 to 714 ± 3 714\pm 3 . On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 ± 0.8 38.0\pm 0.8 to 48.4 ± 2.3 48.4\pm 2.3 , with improvements of 13.4–18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape, offering a mechanistic explanation for the observed performance gains. 1 Introduction Zero-shot reinforcement learning studies the problem of pre-training a single policy on offline, reward-free data such that it can solve any downstream task without further interaction with the environment. It is important because it scales the achievable tasks of a single model without requiring an equal amount of scaling to the training data or online experience, making RL more practical across the diverse and open-ended settings encountered in the real world. A prominent line of work addresses this problem through successor features and task encoders, where a latent representation of states is learned such that any reward function can be expressed as a linear function of that representation Barreto et al. (2017) ; Touati and Ollivier (2021) . At test time, a small set of labeled transitions suffices to recover a task vector via linear regression, which is then used to retrieve the corresponding pre-trained policy. Recent zero-shot RL methods have explored a diverse range of objectives for constructing task representations. Laplacian representations capture the geometry of the environment through eigenfunctions of its transition graph Wu et al. (2018) , while ICVF learns representations through intention-conditioned value prediction Ghosh et al. (2023) . HILP instead organizes the latent space around temporal distances for goal reaching Park et al. (2024) . Self-predictive approaches such as BYOL and BYOL- γ \gamma have also been adapted to the successor-feature setting by predicting future latent representations over one or multiple time scales Grill et al. (2020) ; Lawson et al. (2025) . More recent methods, including RLDP and TD-JEPA, improve multi-step latent-dynamics prediction through chained or temporal-difference objectives Jajoo et al. (2026) ; Bagatella et al. (2025) . Although these approaches differ in how they learn task-relevant structure, they all ultimately rely on the learned task representation to support accurate linear reward inference at test time. Despite this progress, a critical bottleneck has received comparatively little attention. When the task encoder spreads reward-predictive information diffusely across all latent dimensions, the predicted reward landscape is less concentrated near the goal. The resulting reward signal has a weaker gradient to follow, leading to degraded downstream performance. We find that this difference in landscape sharpness persists across a wide range of labeled-set sizes, suggesting it reflects a structural property of the encoder geometry. We address these challenges through a sparsity penalty for the task encoding representation to concentrate its reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of its latent space. We instantiate this idea as Sparse-TD-JEPA , a single-line code addition based on TD-JEPA framework that significantly improves performance on various navigation, locomotion, and puzzle tasks. Empirically, this simple modification produces consistent gains across all 13 evaluated domain-level comparisons. On DeepMind-Control (DMC) , Sparse TD-JEPA improves the average return from 661 ± 6 661\pm 6 to 714 ± 3 714\pm 3 , a gain of 53 points. On OGBench , it raises the average success rate from 38.0 ± 0.8 38.0\pm 0.8 to 48.4 ± 2.3 48.4\pm 2.3 , an absolute improvement of 10.4 percentage points. Moreover, analysis experiment shows that the resulting encoder produces a sharper, more peaked predicted reward landscape, giving the downstream policy a clearer signal to follow. Our contributions are as follows: • We demonstrate theoretically and empirically that ℓ 1 \ell_{1} sparsity on the task encoder improves zero-shot reinforcement learning performance. • Through controlled analysis experiments, we show that the sparsity-penalized task encoder produces a smoother and more informative reward landscape. • We evaluate our method across standard zero-shot reinforcement learning benchmarks covering robotic locomotion, navigation, and manipulation tasks. We demonstrate consistent gains over the base method and other established zero-shot baselines. 2 Related Work Latent-predictive representation learning. The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) LeCun and others (2022) is a representations learning architecture that splits an input into a context view and a target view, then trains a predictor to map the context encoding to the target encoding in a shared latent space. This principle has been instantiated across modalities. Image-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA) Assran et al. (2023) applies it to static images. It uses an asymmetric context/target-encoder design to predict the representations of masked image regions from visible patches. Video-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (V-JEPA) Bardes et al. (2024) ; Assran et al. (2025) extends this to video. It predicts masked spatio-temporal tokens from unmasked ones and supports downstream robotic planning without task-specific reward. Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) Bagatella et al. (2025) instantiates the same context-target prediction problem in reinforcement learning. A state encoder and a task encoder are trained via a temporal-difference latent-predictive loss over offline, off-policy transitions. The predictor is conditioned on the action and a policy latent. Zero-shot reinforcement learning. Zero-shot Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods are methods that pre-train an agent once on offline, reward-free data, then at test time solve arbitrary downstream tasks without further interaction. Most zero-shot RL methods learn a task encoder alongside successor features . The task encoder maps states to a space in which any reward is linear. The successor features predict how much of each task-encoder dimension a policy accumulates over time. Forward-Backward (FB) representations Touati and Ollivier (2021) , a zero-shot RL method, learns both jointly via a bilinear decomposition of successor measures. Other zero-shot reinforcement learning methods construct the task encoder through different objectives. Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) Grill et al. (2020) predicts an encoder’s own future latents. The Laplacian representation Wu et al. (2018) uses eigenfunctions of the environment’s transition graph. The Intention-Conditioned Value Function (ICVF) Ghosh et al. (2023) method uses an implicit value-based objective. HILbert foundation Policy (HILP) Park et al. (2024) enforces distance-preservation for goal-reaching. Regularized Latent Dynamics Prediction (RLDP) Jajoo et al. (2026) uses chained multi-step latent prediction. BYOL- γ \gamma Lawson et al. (2025) extends BYOL to multi-step targets. TD-JEPA Bagatella et al. (2025) uses a temporal-difference latent-predictive objective as the core training signal for both encoders. It distills zero-shot policies end to end. Sparse and structured representation learning. Sparsity-inducing penalties encourage weights or activations toward zero. We refer to Hoefler et al. (2021) for a survey. A useful distinction is between model sparsity , which permanently removes structural elements, and ephemeral sparsity , which sparsifies activations per-example without altering the architecture. Dropout Srivastava et al. (2014) applies ephemeral sparsity to hidden units for regularization. k k -sparse autoencoders Makhzani and Frey (2013) retain only the top- k k activations per example for unsupervised feature learning. Closer to our motivation, Liu et al. (2019) show that ephemeral sparsity in the last hidden layer of a control network improves value-function learning on classic control tasks. It reduces activation overlap between unrelated states. This mitigates interference during bootstrapping. Sparse TD-JEPA improves over the dense baseline in almost every evaluated domain, and our analyses tie these gains to a sharper, more goal-concentrated inferred reward that persists across labeled-set sizes. Future work includes applying the sparsity penalty to other successor-feature-based zero-shot RL methods beyond TD-JEPA, and leveraging the resulting sparse, low-effective-dimension task embeddings for mechanistic interpretability of what individual latent dimensions encode.
